title: Kidney Donation: You Could Be A Saint!
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss kidney donation in the United States. They cover kidney statistics (chronic kidney disease prevalence, the transplant waiting list of roughly 90,000, and deaths while waiting), kidney function and its roles in filtering blood, producing erythropoietin, activating vitamin D and regulating blood pressure, and the main causes of kidney disease (diabetes and high blood pressure). They explain chronic kidney disease stages, dialysis, racial disparities in kidney failure, and how the transplant network and organ matching work, including blood type, size, geography, and scoring. They describe how to sign up as an organ donor, the history of kidney transplantation from 1902 to the 1960s, living versus deceased donation, paired kidney exchanges and donor chains (Alvin Roth), the surgical process and recovery, anti-rejection drugs, and the US ban on paying for organs (National Organ Transplant Act of 1984) and arguments for and against compensating donors. The episode ends with a listener mail about a dB Cooper follow-up story and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening and kidney disease statistics
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and the Dave-researched statistics: about 37 million American adults with chronic kidney disease, about 90,000 people on the kidney transplant list, and roughly 8,000 deaths or disqualifications per year.

segments.title: What kidneys do
segments.summary: Kidneys filter about 200 quarts of fluid a day, contain roughly one to one and a half million nephrons, release erythropoietin and renin, and activate vitamin D. The hosts also explain why about 64 ounces of water a day matters.

segments.title: Causes of kidney disease and stages
segments.summary: Diabetes is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease and high blood pressure is second. The disease is called silent because early stages have no symptoms. Stage five is kidney failure, with waste buildup and symptoms.

segments.title: Racial disparities and dialysis
segments.summary: Black Americans are reported to be four times more likely to have kidney failure than white Americans, with Hispanic and Native American rates also higher. Hosts discuss access to healthcare and money as factors. Dialysis is described as a machine doing the kidneys' filtering, usually about four hours three times a week.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the next segment.

segments.title: Transplant network and organ matching
segments.summary: Patients join the transplant list through the OPTN, managed by UNOS. Matching depends on blood type, organ size, geography and a computer-calculated score that considers age, urgency and other factors. A pool-based system is described as fairer.

segments.title: How to become an organ donor and donation statistics
segments.summary: Donors can say yes at the DMV or register at RegisterMe.org. Around 40,000 transplants occur per year, most are kidneys, and about two-thirds of kidney transplants come from deceased donors. One donor can save up to eight lives. The hosts briefly digress into movies.

segments.title: History of kidney transplantation
segments.summary: Timeline from a 1902 dog kidney transplant in Austria, 1909 monkey experiments, a 1939 attempt in Russia, a 1953 temporary transplant in Paris, Joseph Murray's 1954 long-term twin transplant, and the first non-related transplant in 1962.

segments.title: Living donation and paired exchanges
segments.summary: Living donors are about a quarter of donations and most are related. Living donor kidneys tend to last longer and have less rejection. Paired exchanges and donor chains, developed by Alvin Roth, can link up to around 70 recipients from one altruistic donor.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the surgery discussion.

segments.title: Donor surgery, recovery and anti-rejection drugs
segments.summary: Donors must be at least 18 and healthy. Nephrectomy is often laparoscopic, and the donor's remaining kidney is typically left in place. Recovery is a few days in hospital and six to eight weeks total. Anti-rejection drugs (induction and maintenance agents) are used, and a study of about 17,000 donors reported very low surgical mortality and no increased long-term kidney failure risk. Life insurance protections are noted.

segments.title: Ban on paying for organs
segments.summary: US law (the National Organ Transplant Act) bars financial gain from organ donation, prompted by a Virginia doctor's proposed organ brokerage. Hosts discuss arguments for and against paying donors, including cost savings and black-market concerns, and an Iranian study of paid donors.

segments.title: Listener mail: dB Cooper follow-up and sign-off
segments.summary: Listener Holly shares a family story about the FBI tapping her grandparents' phones over a suspicion about her grandfather and dB Cooper. The hosts close with a call for family stories and a sign-off.
